segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: So that's a recurring topic on this show. We've had many guests who discuss this topic, but in your specific case, how would you explain, like, you escaped this determinism of sorts.

segments.speaker: speaker_1

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: when it's clear that we have governments who are engaging in a lot of the things that they were always engaging with, but now in a sort of new area of cyber,

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: And we haven't really learned. If anything, we've gotten more hungry and avaricious for that information dominance than more towards trying to protect information assurance of our own states.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: So we're getting hungrier for signals intelligence.

segments.text: Do you have an opinion on that? Like, how would you explain this passivity, this lack of change in the legislation area?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Right. Yeah, yeah. I've heard that as well. Yeah.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: Yeah, I forget who that quote is, but I mean, that's really the case that should be applied here. We just don't apply it with any form of rigor.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Part of that I think is the idea that the general public doesn't really have clear visibility on what's happening. Or

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: it has access to this information, but it doesn't necessarily have clarity, it doesn't necessarily understand because it's a very complex topic.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: Well, I think the problem really is also that people still feel, and I'm amazed by that, that they still, like, kind of sit in the camp of, "I have nothing to hide."

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: Or, you know, "They're not after me."

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: "That's fine." You know? It's just—

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Or, "It's worth it because of the terrorists."

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: Yeah, yeah. And to be honest, like, they're probably not after you, but that you have nothing to hide is not true, and that you are taken in the maelstrom of all of the collection that's happening, that's really the concern.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: And is that acceptable? Is that the type of country or state that we want to live in?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: Well, the real thing that you have to worry about... Look, and for most countries in Europe, we live in a democratic state, and there's a lot of emphasis on civil liberties, thank goodness.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: But I think the issue that you have to be afraid of is that in places where this type of power goes unchecked, it leads to the use of this type of data for political purposes,

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: to suppress free speech, to prevent free trials, to follow journalists, to do all kinds of evil things that we would associate with a dictatorship.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: And one could argue, "No, you can trust us with it because we're good."

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Right.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: But the... without a checks and balance, without actually being able to know it, and that's why, you know, then there isn't mass surveillance, there's targeted lawful interception.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: That's why we want those kinds of privacy preserving principles where every use of power is given by a valid authority. And that mass collection could lead to more problems than that it actually solves.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Have we seen, have we witnessed cases of this power being abused?

segments.speaker: speaker_1

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: it will be used and not always by the correct actor that it was intended for.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: That we've seen across different geographies in Europe.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: You know, it can go far back as, I think it was 2000, 2009 or 2012, but we saw the issue in Greece with the lawful intercept equipment that was kept there, where the auditing trails were turned off and it was being used by a host of

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: other actors than the legitimate ones, to follow all types of people.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: We see those powers being abused, sometimes to follow particular, like, political parties, or journalists. There was an investigation actually, I think we need coffee, but—

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: No, but we know about all types of things that are not in Europe, right?

segments.speaker: speaker_0

segments.text: Right

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Yeah

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: So not easy to go and get an order to go and intercept the communications there. What they saw, though, was that the target was using communications provided by BICS, Belgacom International Carrier Services.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: So in order to get to the data of BICS,

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: instead of going through, like, Five Eyes, Nine Eyes, and all types of different MLAT, mutual legal assistance things, they hacked into BICS, which is part of Belgacom, in order to get to the data of that final target.

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: The way that they hacked into them is they used

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: zero-days, which are, like, cyber weapons, if you will. But they're basically vulnerabilities in hardware and software which the maker of the hardware and software doesn't know about, and they are then revealed in the wild-

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: But the UK and the United States, this is not the usual-

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Right

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: ... pocket where you would expect that type of behavior. So it came as a sort of awakening, really a wake-up call, for the telecommunications industry in Europe to be aware that they are also after our data.

segments.text: Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Right

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: ... anything wrong. And if I did, we would not allow it to be put on our networks. So we are paranoid, not just about Huawei, but also about Microsoft, also about Nokia, where we test everything, and that's my preferred response as a CISO-

segments.text: Right

segments.speaker: speaker_1
segments.text: ... to say, be suspicious of all of it.

segments.speaker: speaker_0

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: inspired me to write the book, but it's not the case.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: But in fact, it tells its own story, which is that the tech agenda is still far too low down our list of priorities, and it needs to be higher.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: It's gotten higher in the last few years because of what happened with Brexit and Trump, but it needs to be far, far higher.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And in fact, one of the reasons I wrote the book was 'cause I was so surprised that in both my study of politics at university and in my work in politics, which wasn't for very long but was a formative period,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I found that technology was little understood and even less cared about.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And to the extent that it was cared about, it was really all about how do we use tech to win elections rather than the bigger, deeper political questions posed by technology, which is actually about how it's transforming society itself.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Mm-hmm. Right. That's definitely something we can get into. If we take a look at how technology interacts with politics, if we take a look at the past before we have a look at the future,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: it's pretty easy to take a look at the situation with, I don't know, like, President Kennedy, who was, as it's very well known,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: very charismatic on TV, and that's part of the story, is that's what allowed him to get elected.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And this kind of story is very easy to wrap our minds around. It's very simple. It ...

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: One sentence, and that's it. When we take a look at the current situation, something like Cambridge Analytica and how that is part of what allowed Donald Trump to get elected is much more complex.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: So there's definitely a sense that the complexity is much, much higher than what it used to be. Machine learning famously produces code that humans simply can't read or can't understand.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: We're getting the feeling that we can no longer grasp the inner workings of our democracies, of our societies, of our election systems.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I know it's not an easy question, but can we ever overcome this complexity, this barrier that stands between us and our democracy?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Yes, we can. Just because technologies are complicated doesn't mean that our moral and political ideas about technology have to be complicated.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: In fact, the fact that a machine learning system of the kind you just described is impossible for humans to interpret

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: might, for instance, be a very good reason for not using it in determining the length of someone's jail sentence or whether they should be entitled to a particular social welfare benefit.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: You might say precisely because it's so complex that the political consequence of that is that it's not an appropriate way to use that technology.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And so what I try to do in my book is draw pretty simple conclusions about technologies like the one I've just described, which can guide us in their use.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Looking back to the past, as you say, the trend that I identify going even further back is this: that when we have big changes in the way that we store and communicate information,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: we also tend to have big changes in our political structures as well.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: So go way back, for instance, to the invention of writing, cuneiform tablets they were called, in the walled cities that were in what is now Iraq, on the edge of the Euphrates River.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: They're some of the earliest forms of writing we have. It appears that in the decades following the invention of writing,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: the very first empires were formed, stretching over large territories,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: and the reason that happened was because there hadn't previously been a stable enough way of storing and communicating information about tax and grain storage or whatever else it was until writing as a permanent medium was invented.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And so the invention of this technology, this information technology, changed politics. So did the invention of the printing press, so did the invention of the internet, and so too will other digital inventions.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And the reason this happens isn't that complicated. Politics is about communication. Communication is the very, very heart and soul of human politics.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: It's what makes it different from what animals do in the animal kingdom,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: in its levels of sophistication. And so we shouldn't be surprised that when the way that we store and communicate information changes, the way that we organize ourselves based on that communication changes as well.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: So it would be naive of us, I think, to suppose that things are gonna stay similar or stay the same. One thing that struck me is when you mentioned we should not be using machine learning algorithms to decide,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: for instance, of the jail sentence for an individual.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Was there ever a chance of something like that happening or is that something that we only read about in 1984?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: It does happen. I mean, the point I was making, first of all, was not that you shouldn't use these algorithms at all, but if you literally can't explain how a system works— Sure ...

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: then you shouldn't use it. Might be a machine learning system, might be another system. But for instance, there are courts in the United States where if you're being sentenced, they will use a machine learning system to read data about you which

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: purports to predict how likely you are to reoffend.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And the judge, it doesn't determine your sentence, but the judge is entitled to take that into account when he sentences you or when she sentences you.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And there's been quite a lot of legal upset about that in the United States, particularly because the Supreme Court of Wisconsin

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: argued that it was lawful to use such systems

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: even when the person being sentenced wasn't able to access the data and algorithms that had been used in part to calculate the length of their sentence, and the American Supreme Court declined to hear the case.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: So yes, this stuff is real. Right. I mean, algorithms are also used for things like predictive policing, or to determine whether certain prisoners get bail.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I can't think of any society in which they are currently the last word, so they're not decisive, although they might be in an individual case.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: It certainly sounds very deterministic. It sounds like, based on where you're from, what your name is, what your gender is, these are things that might influence the algorithm and,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: have an important impact on, for instance, your jail sentence.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Exactly. Jamie, are you a pessimist? Should we be scared of the future? Is this the message of your book that we should be scared of what the future has in hold for us?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Not scared, no, and no, I'm not a pessimist, but I can't describe myself as an optimist either. What I say is that it's possible now to see coming over the horizon these big problems, these big challenges.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: What are we gonna do about them? Are we going to let the technologies of tomorrow develop according simply to market logic, getting on with it themselves, or are we going to step in and regulate and legislate and

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: bring them under the control of a wider population for the good of the public?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: If we take that choice, the latter choice, then we'll be in a good position because we'll be able to harness all of the awesome and amazing things that technology can bring us,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: while at the same time preserving and augmenting our democracy and our freedom and our justice.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: But if we simply sit back and let things take their natural course, then there's every reason to be pessimistic because there's no reason why technologies developed according to commercial logic should also be good for society. Mm.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: ... and for politics. There's no reason at all. Part of the challenge, I think, is that

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: most of the innovation we are witnessing in the tech industry comes from Silicon Valley, comes from the United States, which is a place that cherishes this idea of entrepreneurship, of risk-taking, of innovation, and where there is

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: relatively less legislation, less of a tight grip on those companies by the states.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: From what you're saying, it sounds like you're a partisan of more legislation. Do you believe this is something that will happen?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I think your diagnosis is absolutely correct. I think that a lot of the tech that comes out of America comes out of America because of the sort of Wild West nature of the entrepreneurial environment there.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: There's also things like the First Amendment to the US Constitution, which makes it very difficult for states to intervene in the free market where it's considered that it might have implications for free speech.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And yes, the Americans would look towards us here in Europe and they would say, "Have you ever wondered why you don't have a Twitter or a Facebook or a Google?"

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And there's probably some merit in that question. They're getting at something there. I believe that it is up to Europe, as I think it is already doing, to propose and to show through success an alternative model.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I don't think the American way is the only way of doing it. If we want to chuck all our laws down the toilet in pursuit of naked entrepreneurship and the maximization of unicorns and billion-dollar, trillion-dollar companies, then we can,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: but that doesn't mean we should.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And so I think what you'll see, and what I would encourage, is the emergence of basically three global models, the American model, the European model, and the Chinese model.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And I am not shy about arguing for a European model, to answer your question, which involves some regulation, some legislation,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: which on the one hand seeks to preserve an innovative culture and free speech and the like, but on the other hand recognizes that technologies have consequences and that some things are more important than making a quick buck.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: That is a very crude way of putting it, but it's the essence of my argument. Right. In fact, in my next book, if I may— Go ahead ...

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I'll be making the case for regulation and saying, "Here's why we should have regulation. Here's what a regulator should look like, and here's what the regulations themselves should look like."

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And I'm sure it will be greeted with hostility in certain parts of the States. So Europe is certainly a challenge, but to go back for a second to Silicon Valley, how do we even

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: get those tech giants to put themselves in question and to see the danger they can bring to our democracies and our societies, such as in the case of Cambridge Analytica?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Do we have any hope that such a thing could happen? Putting it simply, sometimes tech firms will just do the right thing.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: You know, Microsoft claims to follow the GDPR rules even though it's not strictly subject to them in some respects. Good for Microsoft.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Sometimes public outrage will force companies or at least encourage them to take a different path. I think that is the case with Facebook over the last few years.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I'm not saying it's been doing a good job, but it's certainly been taking more public efforts to regulate itself. But I'm very clear about this.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: You can't rely on the benevolence or the wisdom of— Right ... tech firms. And I do think it's a bit of a dodge sometimes.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I think we— Well, as you said, it's kind of a Wild West nature over there, so. Right. But we underestimate sometimes the consequences that national or things like supranational in the form of the EU regulation can have.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: We simply are better protected here in Europe in terms of our data usage because of the GDPR than our brothers and sisters in America are.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: We are better protected, and I'm sure the companies in question find it more onerous to operate in Europe as a consequence, but so be it.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: They still do. It's a huge market. The fact that, for instance, it is very difficult to tax big multinational companies doesn't mean that we don't pass tax law and try to tax them.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: It just means that it's not always 100% successful. Now, I recognize the difficulties with regulating tech firms. The biggest risk is obviously always that you make one area so uncompetitive

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: that it doesn't enjoy the flow of business that other areas might have, which is why continental-wide legislation is preferable to national legislation.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: But at the same time, you know, I think the German government said to Twitter, "It's unlawful to show a swastika in this country, and if you show a swastika, if someone tweets a swastika, we're gonna hold you responsible."

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Lo and behold, if I tweet a swastika in England and someone looks at it in Germany, they won't see it.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: If companies were given incentives to find national solutions to their regulatory problems more often, I suspect, with their great genius, they would find ways of doing so.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: You're saying that the changes we make here in Europe, here in the European Union, however difficult it might be, will at some point have a global effect on what's happening for our brothers and sisters in the US.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Maybe, although that isn't their primary aim. Their primary aim is to— Right ... is to look after people in Europe. Yeah.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And sometimes they do. Part of the challenge here is that, you know, we've seen,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I think it was like about a year ago, Mark Zuckerberg in front of Congress, and he was being asked, "How come your company is able to make money if you're not charging your customers?"

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Obviously, that was an edge case. I'm hoping that our politicians in Europe are a bit more tech-savvy than that. However, that's definitely part of the problem, isn't it?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Again, we're going back to the complexity of these issues, and we're having these lawmakers, which are often kind of the, you know, senior types, and we're asking them to legislate on stuff that's very hard to grasp.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: So isn't that part of the issue, again, the complexity of these,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: of these issues? Yeah. If you're asking me do I have a great deal of confidence in the current generation of lawmakers in the Western world to produce the wise rules and laws that are needed,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: the answer is no, I don't.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: It's partly generational for the reasons you described. There are still— I still meet politicians who will proudly tell me that they don't know how to use email, proudly.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And I just sort of think, "Well, if that's what you take pride in, you're unlikely to be able to say much of use about machine learning algorithms."

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: So it's partly a generational thing. It's partly a political will thing. Politicians now are a lot more educated on climate change than they were 15 years ago.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: The reason for that is 'cause it's risen up the political agenda. It's no longer acceptable not to understand the science, whether you agree or disagree with it.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And I would like to see something similar happening with technology. It's why I do what I do. I don't think you need to be a computer scientist or a software— Mm-hmm ...

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: engineer to understand the social implications of these technologies, but you do need to have a passing understanding of them, which comes from some kind of curiosity.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And you need to have a passing understanding of the literature that's been written about them. And there actually are quite a lot of smart policy types,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: not politicians themselves, but people working for politicians, who are increasingly interested in this stuff.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I have been encouraged by that, but we're nowhere near where we need to be. You are making a comparison with climate change.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: There is a definite urgency with climate issues. I don't think you can say, or can you actually say, that there is a sense of urgency when talking about these tech issues?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Well, it's funny you say that. I mean, I think our generation sees there as being urgency with climate change. Right. I think a lot of people don't see it that way.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I think they think, "So the sea's going to rise a bit at an indeterminate point in the future because of a vast aggregation of different sources of carbon emission across the planet."

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: In a sense, one of the difficulties with climate change is that it lacks an urgency. You can't say, "This time next year, San Francisco will be underwater."

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And to that extent, I think it shares an issue with technology. What you're describing is an incremental process of change with tech, albeit one that I think is accelerating in speed rather than decelerating, and there's no...

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: There are seldom flashpoints where things come to a head. That said, the reason that Zuckerberg was before Congress is because of a sense that there might have been Russian interference in American elections

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: or that Cambridge Analytica had had an unwanted effect on the outcome of those elections.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Likewise, there have been similar rumblings in England after the Brexit referendum, and I make no comment about that. But

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: what I predict is you will have moments of crisis punctuated by long periods of nothingness, and what I try to do in my work is try to raise technology, albeit that it is something that is difficult to grasp, as an urgent policy problem,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: but I want to raise it to the top of the political agenda.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Because if we wait till it's too late, then we'll be in big trouble. One topic we have not been talking about thus far is the idea of privacy.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Six years ago, I think it was, Edward Snowden came forward with his infamous revelations. I don't know about you, but I don't get the feeling that a lot has changed, again, with the common sense of urgency.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I don't see a lot of people around me worrying about their privacy being violated. How do you explain that? It's hard to know what's happening inside the US government and whether there is a more strict approach taken to acts of

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: questionable legality than were in the past.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: So I can't comment on that. I was more talking about the broad population. Yeah. Yeah. I mean, it is an interesting thing that

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: privacy, which I actually think is a bit of a '90s word, I don't find it that helpful a term, but it has never become the dominant political concern that perhaps some people thought it was.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Some people might have seen the Snowden revelations and been glad that that kind of surveillance was taking place and felt safer because of it and not cared because most of it was done by machines rather than by human beings.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: That is a respectable point of view, albeit that many people would disagree with it and say that it should be regulated by law in any event.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: But what's funny is that we have these outbursts of concern about what the state does. The real threat to privacy is from private entities, not the state— Right ...

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: which gather data about us and, and I think a lot of people would be staggered— Right. But— ... if they were showed what private companies knew about them.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: But I will say that part of the Snowden revelations was that the NSA had access to the data being collected by Google, by Microsoft, and so on.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: So you know, it's actually both. Absolutely. And how the state gets its hands on that data is always going to be an interesting question.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Does it get its hands on it commercially by buying it? Does it get its hands on it legally by requiring it? Does it get its hands on it illegally by hacking into it?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: These are all questions which a free society should debate about what the appropriate role of the state is in mass surveillance.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I do think if most people had a sense about what was known about them, they would be surprised, though. Right.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: So again, part of the issue is this complexity, the fact that not everyone understands what's going on. Yeah. Although, how complex is it?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: How complex is it to teach someone that every time they use an app, it gathers data about their location, or every time they take a photo of themselves for a particular app,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: that photo is stored in a database and used to train artificial intelligence systems or might be sold to the government to use to develop face recognition technology to survey the public?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I don't think these concepts would be on the grasp of ordinary people. You don't need to understand how the technology works.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Mm-hmm. But I do think it's all explainable. If it's explainable, how then can we explain the fact that people seem not to care?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Well, maybe some people know about it but don't care. Maybe the fact that it's explainable doesn't necessarily mean that it's been explained.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Right. And you know, I have realistic expectations about what one can do. For instance, in my line of work, I write a book.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Some people will read it, some people won't read it. The contents of it will be reported, but many of its contents won't be reported.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Public education about a topic as big as this is a difficult thing.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: It's particularly difficult in circumstances where a lot of very powerful entities, be them states or corporations, don't really have an interest in public education of this kind, even without being conspiratorial.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: There's just no great social demand for it or commercial demand for it from their perspective. People are just trying to get on with their lives most of the time.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Yeah. The same, you can ask about any political question, why aren't more people angry about this? The answer is because they're just trying to get their kids to school on time.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Right. Again, there is very little urgency in this case. Going back to this idea of an increasingly quantified society of data being collected about everyone all the time, could we take a second and explain to our listeners

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: how dangerous that is and why it's problematic that data is being collected about us all the time, if that is your opinion, of course?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Right. So we generate about as much data every couple of hours now as we did from the dawn of time until 2003, and what it means is that us as individuals, we as individuals leave behind us a

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: data trail of what we buy, where we go, who we hang out with, who we speak to, what we say, what we care about, which paints a very detailed picture of our inner and outer lives,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: which politicians and kings and priests of the past would have been envious of.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: We are revealed to a much greater extent. Like, to a certain extent, it's not a bad thing. A lot of the comfort and creativity that we draw from technology, the useful services that it will provide to us in the future,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: will be precisely because so much data is being gathered and

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: and we are truly known as people, truly understood.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: But at the same time, the more you know about someone, the easier it is to manipulate them and to influence them, and the person doing the manipulating or the influencing might be a commercial entity or it might be a political entity.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: But either way, we are more naked to that kind of power and more defenseless to it than we were in the past. It's probably not a huge problem if we're at least aware of it and can be vigilant against it.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: But for the reasons we were discussing a moment ago, I think a lot of us aren't,

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: and we are therefore endowing certain groups in society, those who have access to that data about us, with enormous power for the future, which they may well use for good ends, but

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: should we be relying on trust?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: It seems like this power, which used to be held by the states, by governments, is often now being held by these tech giants.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Currency is one example with cryptocurrencies, information, the way we are being informed. A couple of decades ago, it used to be the public broadcaster, you know, the BBC was the main way we were all being informed.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Nowadays, it's a Facebook algorithm for most of us. Is this our future? Are we destined to being subjected to this power which is being held by tech giants?

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: I broadly agree in the sense that I think that an increasing amount of power will flow to those who own and control certain technologies.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Now, that power might take a number of forms. It might take the form I was describing a moment ago, which is when people gather data about you, they're able to influence and manipulate you.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: It might take the form of perception control, where the slice of reality that we're presented of the outside world by our news feeds or our search algorithms is very, very slender.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: It's very small, and it determines our sense of right and wrong and true and false, and those who are the gatekeepers for that information, for what we know and understand of the world out there, are very powerful like that as well.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: And there's a third way as well that technology creates power, which is by writing rules that the rest of us have to follow.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: So when you try to send a tweet that is more than 280 characters, you're literally prohibited from doing so because the system won't let you.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: Likewise, your self-driving car might not drive over the speed limit if that's what its coders, if that's what its designers have chosen for it, whereas that's obviously a choice that you might have had in the past.

segments.speaker: speaker_0
segments.text: So yes, I think that kind of power is being increasingly privatized. The only question remains, what do we do about it?
